analysis.one_liner: Bans unconscionably excessive gasoline prices during a proclaimed international oil-market emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, never received a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful to charge unconscionably excessive prices for gasoline and other petroleum fuels once the President proclaims an international crisis affecting oil markets and designates the covered area, which could be the entire country. The FTC would enforce the ban with civil penalties of up to triple the profits gained or $100 million, the Justice Department could seek criminal fines up to $500 million, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents. Enforcement would prioritize companies with more than $10 billion a year in US fuel sales.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and other fuel consumers, including farms, homes, and businesses buying gasoline or heating fuels directly. During a proclaimed emergency, they would gain a federal backstop against sellers charging wildly excessive prices, with the heaviest penalties aimed at the largest companies and states empowered to sue locally.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Motorists and fuel consumers during emergencies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits selling gasoline or other petroleum distillates at unconscionably excessive prices in any area covered by a presidential proclamation of an international crisis affecting oil markets, with the proclamation lasting up to 30 days at a time and renewable.

Lets the FTC enforce the ban with enhanced civil penalties of up to three times the violator's profits or $100 million, and gives the Justice Department authority to seek criminal fines up to $500 million, prioritizing enforcement against companies with over $10 billion in annual US fuel sales.
Authorizes state attorneys general to sue in federal court on behalf of their residents to enforce the ban at the retail level, while leaving state anti-gouging laws untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale and retail sellers of gasoline and other petroleum fuels, above all large oil companies and chains with more than $10 billion in annual US fuel sales, who would face enhanced civil penalties and criminal fines for excessive pricing during proclaimed emergencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large fuel sellers and oil companies

drawbacks.text: The ban only applies after the President personally proclaims an international crisis affecting oil markets and designates the covered area, so ordinary price spikes outside such a proclaimed emergency would not be covered and protection would depend on presidential discretion.

Price ceilings during a genuine supply shortage can discourage sellers from bringing extra fuel to the affected area, although the bill partly addresses this by treating a failure to increase quantities sold after the proclamation as a factor in judging whether a price was unconscionable.

The unconscionably excessive standard relies on comparisons to the seller's own prior prices and competitors' prices, which could invite litigation over what counts as grossly excessive and pull enforcement priorities during an emergency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is real but narrow: it only operates during a proclaimed oil-market emergency, and the largest companies would face genuine financial exposure. The main tradeoff is the risk that price ceilings complicate supply responses during a shortage, which the bill's quantity-increase factor tries to mitigate but cannot eliminate. As drafted, the potential savings for consumers in an emergency outweigh those risks for most buyers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to a subcommittee the next day, and never advanced to a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Harder introduced the bill on April 7, 2022, during a period of sharply elevated gasoline prices following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 7, 2022, and to its Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce on April 8, 2022.
The bill attracted no cosponsors and received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale and retail fuel sellers, who avoided a new federal price-gouging ban with penalties aimed at the largest companies, plus no one else; consumers gained nothing because the protection never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fuel sellers, who avoided new penalties

for.name: Rep. Josh Harder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee without a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 8, 2022, and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan measure exists beyond that.

industries.note: During a proclaimed oil-market emergency they would face civil penalties up to triple profits or $100 million and criminal fines up to $500 million for unconscionably excessive prices, with enforcement prioritized against companies over $10 billion in annual US fuel sales. The bill died before any of this took effect.

Retail sales to motorists, farms, homes, and businesses would be directly covered, and state attorneys general could sue retailers in federal court. Existing state gouging laws would remain intact under the bill's non-preemption clause.
